q: What engine is installed in this airplane?
a: A Lycoming O-320 rated 160 horsepower at 2700 RPM. POH 1.3 and 2.7 both approve either the O-320-D2A or the O-320-D3G, exactly as TCDS 2A13 does, and the FAA registry records this airplane's engine only as 0-320 SERIES. So the installed dash number has to be read off the engine data plate rather than asserted from the book.

q: Your instructor says the type certificate names the D3G. Is that right?
a: Only half right. The TCDS and the handbook both approve either engine; neither picks one. POH 1.3(c) and 2.7(c) print O-320-D2A or O-320-D3G side by side, and the registry entry for this airplane says only 0-320 SERIES. The correct answer in an oral is that both are approved for the model and mine is whichever is stamped on the data plate, which I would read before quoting it.

q: How much power does this engine make, and at what RPM?
a: 160 horsepower at 2700 RPM. The handbook says it three times: 1.3 rated horsepower 160, 2.7 maximum horsepower 160, and 7.5 rated at 160 HP at 2700 RPM. The tachometer red line is also 2700 RPM and is labeled maximum continuous power, so there is no separate higher takeoff rating to manage and no time limit to watch.

q: Describe the engine's basic configuration.
a: In the handbook's own words at 1.3, it is four cylinder, direct drive, horizontally opposed, air cooled. Direct drive means there is no reduction gearbox, so propeller RPM equals crankshaft RPM. Section 7.5 repeats it as a four cylinder, direct drive, horizontally opposed engine. It is carbureted rather than fuel injected, and normally aspirated.

q: What is the engine's displacement, and where does the name O-320 come from?
a: 319.8 cubic inches, POH 1.3. The Lycoming designation rounds that off: O for horizontally opposed, 320 for the approximate displacement in cubic inches. The absence of a prefix letter is the point worth making, because it says there is no gearing, no supercharging and no fuel injection, which is exactly the direct drive, carbureted, normally aspirated engine the handbook describes.

q: What is the compression ratio, and why does it matter on a Warrior?
a: 8.5:1, POH 1.3. It is the figure that separates the 160 hp D-series engine in this Warrior II from the 150 hp 7.00:1 engine in the earlier PA-28-151 Warrior, and the two airplanes look identical on the ramp. It also ties to the fuel: a higher compression ratio needs the higher octane, which is why the filler is placarded 100 or 100LL aviation grade and lower grades are not allowed.

q: How is this engine cooled?
a: By air. POH 7.5: engine air enters on either side of the propeller through openings in a nose cowling and is carried through the engine baffling around the engine and the oil cooler. The same baffled air cools the cylinders and the cooler, so there is no separate scoop for the oil. The preflight includes checking the engine baffle seals in the nose section.

q: Does this airplane have cowl flaps? If not, what controls engine temperature?
a: No cowl flaps at all. The cooling air is ducted by fixed baffling, so temperature is controlled by what the pilot does: lowering the nose for more airspeed and more cooling flow, keeping the mixture rich in the climb, and reducing the climb angle. On a hot day the tools are a shallower climb and a richer mixture, not a lever.

q: What are the engine mounts made of, and what is a dynafocal mount for?
a: POH 7.5: the engine mounts are constructed of steel tubing, and dynafocal mounts are provided to reduce vibration. Section 7.3 notes the steel tube engine mount is one of the few parts of the primary structure that is not aluminum alloy. A dynafocal arrangement aims the rubber isolators at the engine's center of gravity, so vibration is absorbed in the mounts instead of being fed into the airframe.

q: Trace the induction air path from outside the airplane to the cylinders.
a: POH 7.5: carburetor induction air enters a chin scoop on the lower right cowling and is passed through a wetted polyurethane filter to the carburetor air box, then through the carburetor and the intake manifold to the cylinders. It is an updraft, carbureted, normally aspirated installation, so there is no turbocharger and no automatic alternate air door; the only alternate path is carburetor heat.

q: Tell me about the induction air filter.
a: POH 8.11: a wet-type polyurethane foam filter, in the lower right front of the engine compartment behind four quarter-turn fasteners. It must be inspected at least once every 50 hours, and more frequently in dusty conditions. It is disposable, so if it is excessively dirty or shows any damage it is replaced rather than cleaned.

q: What do you know about the carburetor, and what does the handbook not tell you?
a: It is a float-type carburetor fed from a carburetor air box, with the throttle and mixture acting at it and a screen at its inlet cleaned every 50 hours; Figure 7-9 simply labels it CARBURETOR. What the handbook never gives is the make, model or float type, and the TCDS gives only carburetor settings, so I would not name a manufacturer in the oral. That is a case where the honest answer is better than a confident guess.

q: Where does carburetor heat air come from?
a: From a shroud around the muffler. POH 7.5: air for the muffler shroud is picked up from the nose cowling and carried through a duct to the shroud, and heated air enters the carburetor air box through a hose connected to the heater shroud. The same dual mufflers and heater shrouds supply cabin heat, the defroster and what Piper calls the carburetor deicing system.

q: Is the air you get with carburetor heat filtered?
a: No, and the handbook says so. POH 4.19: avoid prolonged ground operation with carburetor heat ON as the air is unfiltered. The heated air comes off the muffler shroud, downstream of the induction filter, so with heat selected the engine is breathing whatever dust is around. That is why the ground check of carb heat is brief and why heat comes off before takeoff.

q: Describe the carburetor heat control.
a: POH 7.11: a lever to the right of the control quadrant on the instrument panel, placarded with two positions, ON down and OFF up. It is an on-off control, not a modulating one. That is precisely why the handbook insists on full heat; there is no approved intermediate setting for the pilot to select.

q: Why does Piper say never to use partial carburetor heat?
a: POH 3.41 NOTE: partial carburetor heat may be worse than no heat at all, since it may melt part of the ice which will refreeze in the intake system. The handbook's rule is that when using carburetor heat always use full heat, and when the ice is removed return the control to the full cold position. Section 3.29 says the same thing: heat should be full on when carburetor ice is encountered.

q: In what conditions does this handbook say carburetor ice can form?
a: POH 3.29: under certain moist atmospheric conditions at temperatures of minus 5 degrees C to 20 degrees C, it is possible for ice to form in the induction system, even in summer weather. The cause it gives is the high air velocity through the carburetor venturi and the heat absorbed by vaporization of the fuel. That band is type specific and it includes temperatures below freezing.

q: What is the first indication of carburetor ice in this airplane?
a: A drop in RPM. POH 3.41: engine roughness is usually due to carburetor icing, which is indicated by a drop in RPM and may be accompanied by a slight loss of airspeed or altitude. The propeller is fixed pitch and there is no manifold pressure gauge on the panel, so the tachometer is the instrument that moves first.

q: Why is the carburetor ice indication different in a constant speed airplane?
a: Because a governor holds the RPM. With a fixed pitch propeller, a loss of power lets the propeller slow, so the tachometer falls and that is the cue. With a constant speed propeller the governor flattens the blades to hold the selected RPM, so the tachometer stays where it was and the loss appears as falling manifold pressure instead. This airplane has no manifold pressure gauge, so RPM is all there is.

q: You suspect carburetor ice and apply full heat. What should happen?
a: It gets worse before it gets better. POH 3.41: RPM will decrease slightly and roughness will increase; then wait for a decrease in roughness or an increase in RPM, indicating ice removal. If there is no change in approximately one minute, return the carburetor heat to OFF. Adjust the mixture for maximum smoothness meanwhile. If too much ice is allowed to accumulate, restoration of full power may not be possible.

q: Do you put carburetor heat on for every approach in this airplane?
a: Piper says no. POH 4.31: carburetor heat should not be applied unless there is an indication of carburetor icing, since the use of carburetor heat causes a reduction in power which may be critical in case of a go-around, and full throttle operation with carburetor heat on can cause detonation. That is this handbook's position and it differs from the habit many pilots are taught.

q: What does the POH want you to do for a prolonged power-off descent?
a: POH 4.29: apply full carburetor heat before the power reduction if icing conditions are suspected, retard the throttle, lean the mixture as required, and verify power response approximately every 30 seconds by partially opening and then closing the throttle, which is clearing the engine. Leveling off, enrich the mixture, set power as required and select carb heat off unless icing is still suspected.

q: What is detonation, and what does this handbook say can cause it?
a: Detonation is uncontrolled, explosive burning of the charge after the spark instead of a smooth flame front, and it drives cylinder pressure and temperature up fast enough to damage pistons, rings and cylinders. This handbook names one cause directly, at 4.31: full throttle operation with carburetor heat on can cause detonation. The other guards are the placarded minimum fuel grade and not running lean at high power.

q: How does preignition differ from detonation?
a: Preignition is ignition of the charge before the spark, by a hot spot such as a glowing deposit or a damaged plug, so the mixture burns against a piston that is still rising; detonation is a violent burn after normal ignition. Preignition can destroy a cylinder very quickly. This handbook does not discuss preignition at all, so I would offer that as general engine knowledge and take the detail from the Lycoming operator's manual.

q: How many magnetos does this engine have, and what else does the engine drive?
a: Two magnetos. POH 7.5 lists the engine as equipped with a starter, a 60 amp 14 volt alternator, a shielded ignition, two magnetos, vacuum pump drive, a fuel pump and a wetted polyurethane foam induction air filter. That list is the right answer to what the engine drives, and it is what tells you the vacuum gyros and the ignition survive a loss of the electrical system.

q: Why does the engine have two magnetos?
a: For redundancy and for power. Two independent ignition systems mean a failed magneto, lead or plug does not stop the engine, and firing the cylinder from two plugs gives two flame fronts, so the charge burns faster and more completely. The handbook never states a plug count, so the honest version is two per cylinder, one fired by each magneto, confirmed from the engine manual rather than claimed from the POH.

q: Why does the engine keep running with the master switch off?
a: Because a magneto is engine driven and self-exciting: it makes its own current from a rotating magnet and needs nothing from the airplane's electrical system. That is why the ignition does not appear in the POH 7.15 list of standard electrical accessories, and why an alternator failure, a flat battery or an electrical fire handled with master off still leaves you with a running engine.

q: How are the magnetos driven?
a: Off the engine. POH 7.5 lists the two magnetos among the engine-driven accessories alongside the vacuum pump drive, which points to accessory gear drive, but the handbook never states the drive arrangement in words. The safe answer is the principle, that they are engine driven and self-exciting and so need no electrical power, with the gearing detail taken from the engine manual.

q: Does this engine have an impulse coupling, and what does it do?
a: An impulse coupling winds a spring at cranking speed and snaps the magnet through, giving a late, hot spark for starting. The words impulse coupling appear nowhere in this handbook. What it does say, at Operating Tip 10.3(j), is that the magneto selector should be placed to LEFT during hand starting to reduce the probability of kick back, and the Lycoming parts catalog lists one plain and one impulse magneto, which points to the left one.
dup: What is an impulse coupling and why is it needed?

q: Which spark plugs does each magneto fire?
a: The handbook does not say. POH 7.5 gives only a shielded ignition and two magnetos; there is no plug count and no harness assignment anywhere in the book. The right answer is two plugs per cylinder, one fired by each magneto, confirmed from the engine manual, rather than inventing a top-and-bottom split. That is a stronger answer than a confident wrong one.

q: What does a shielded ignition mean, and why is it fitted?
a: POH 7.5 describes the installation as having a shielded ignition. Shielding is metal braid over the leads and plug caps that contains the radio frequency noise a magneto system throws off, so it does not reach the radios and navigation receivers as a buzz that rises and falls with engine speed. The handbook gives no further detail on the harness than that phrase.

q: You pull the mixture to shut down and the engine keeps running. What does that mean?
a: A magneto is not being grounded, normally a broken or disconnected P-lead, so that magneto is live no matter where the key is. From then on the propeller is treated as hot: nobody touches it, the mixture stays at idle cut-off, fuel selector and master go off, and the airplane is written up before any blade is turned. It is the same defect that shows as a zero drop in the run-up.

q: At what RPM do you check the magnetos?
a: 2000 RPM. POH 4.19 says the magnetos should be checked at 2000 RPM, and the Section 4 GROUND CHECK list opens with throttle 2000 RPM. That is a published figure in this handbook rather than a school checklist number, and it is the same RPM at which the vacuum gauge should read 4.8 to 5.1 inches of mercury.

q: What are the magneto drop limits in the run-up?
a: POH 4.19: drop off on either magneto should not exceed 175 RPM, and the difference between the magnetos should not exceed 50 RPM. Both are on the GROUND CHECK list as max. drop 175 RPM and max. diff. 50 RPM. The handbook adds a limit hardly anyone quotes: operation on one magneto should not exceed 10 seconds.
dup: How do you carry out a magneto check and what are the limits?

q: Is there a time limit on running on one magneto?
a: Yes. POH 4.19: operation on one magneto should not exceed 10 seconds. The handbook gives no reason, but the practical one is that extended single-magneto running at run-up power fouls the plugs that are not firing. It makes the check deliberately brisk: left, back to both, right, back to both, watching the drop and the split.

q: What does an excessive magneto drop tell you?
a: That one ignition system is not carrying its share: fouled or failed plugs, a bad lead or a magneto out of time. A drop beyond 175 RPM, or a split beyond 50 RPM, means the airplane does not go as it is. A rough-running magneto with a big drop usually points at a fouled plug, and the normal first attempt is to lean at higher RPM to burn the deposit off and recheck before calling maintenance.

q: What does no RPM drop at all on the magneto check mean?
a: That the check did not actually isolate a magneto, which is a grounding fault in the switch or the P-lead, so that magneto is live all the time and the propeller is hot. A zero drop is a defect, not a good sign. The small drop is the evidence that the system was really switched off; without it the airplane is written up before flight.
dup: What does an excessive magneto drop mean, and what does no drop at all mean?

q: What RPM drop should you see on the carburetor heat check?
a: This handbook does not publish one. The GROUND CHECK list says only carburetor heat check, and 4.19 gives the reasons without a number: to be sure the control is operating properly and to clear any ice formed during taxiing. So I look for a definite drop and a clean recovery, and I would say the POH specifies no figure rather than quote a school number as if it came from the book.

q: How is the starter operated?
a: From the ignition switch. POH 4.15: engage the starter by rotating the magneto switch clockwise, and when the engine fires release the magneto switch, so it is spring loaded off the key and not a separate button. Operating Tip 10.3(e) adds that radio, light and pitot heat switches should be checked off before engaging the starter so as not to create an overloaded condition.

q: Describe the exhaust system and what else it feeds.
a: POH 7.5: the exhaust system is constructed of stainless steel and incorporates dual mufflers with heater shrouds to supply heated air for the cabin, the defroster system and the carburetor deicing system. So the exhaust is not just plumbing; everything warm on this airplane comes off it, which is why a cracked muffler is at once a carbon monoxide problem and a carburetor heat problem.

q: Describe the throttle control.
a: POH 7.11: a lever on the control quadrant in the lower center of the instrument panel, accessible to both pilot and copilot, running on teflon-lined control cables, used to adjust engine RPM. On a fixed pitch airplane the throttle is the only power lever and the tachometer is the power instrument; there is no propeller control and no manifold pressure gauge to set.

q: What does the mixture control do, and how do you stop this engine?
a: POH 7.11: the mixture control lever adjusts the air to fuel ratio, and the engine is shut down by placing the mixture lever in the full lean position, that is idle cut-off. Shutting down on the mixture leaves no combustible charge in the cylinders, so the magnetos can then be switched off into a dead engine. The control lock has to be disengaged before the lever will come back.

q: What is the friction lock for?
a: POH 7.11: a friction adjustment lever on the right side of the control quadrant that increases or decreases the friction holding the throttle and mixture, or locks them in a selected position. It is set loose enough that the levers move deliberately and tight enough that they do not creep back on their own in the climb or in cruise.

q: Does this airplane have a primer, and why is it on the emergency checklists?
a: POH 7.13 calls it an optional engine priming system, with the pump immediately to the left of the throttle quadrant; in practice it is fitted, since primer locked appears on the placarded takeoff checklist, in Before Takeoff and in both engine failure checklists. An unlocked primer can feed raw fuel into the induction system and run the engine rough or rich, which is why it gets checked when power is lost.

q: How do you lean this engine in cruise?
a: POH 4.27: reduce to the desired cruise power setting and lean the mixture to peak RPM, then adjust the throttle if necessary for the final RPM setting; leaning to peak engine RPM gives best fuel economy. There is no EGT as standard equipment, so peak RPM is the handbook's leaning reference on this airplane, and 7.11 and 7.5 both send the pilot to the Lycoming operator's manual for more.

q: Do you ever take off with the mixture less than full rich?
a: POH 4.21 NOTE: the mixture should be set FULL RICH, but a minimum amount of leaning is permitted for smooth engine operation when taking off at high elevation. So full rich is the rule and leaning for takeoff is a density altitude exception, leaned only as far as smooth running. On approach 4.31 wants full rich as well, to ensure maximum acceleration if the throttle has to be opened again.

q: Tell me about the propeller.
a: A Sensenich two-blade fixed pitch propeller of aluminum alloy construction, model 74DM6-0-60 or 74DM6-0-58 per POH 2.7. Section 7.5 gives a 74-inch diameter with a 58 or 60-inch pitch, the pitch determined at 75 percent of the diameter. Fixed pitch is why RPM is the power indication, why an RPM drop is the first sign of carb ice, and why there is no propeller lever in the cockpit.

q: What static RPM should this engine make, and why does it matter?
a: POH 2.7 gives it by propeller model, at sea level in standard conditions at maximum permissible throttle: for the 74DM6-0-60, not above 2430 RPM and not below 2330 RPM; for the 74DM6-0-58, not above 2465 and not below 2365. It is the check that engine and propeller together are making rated power. The handbook refers to the maintenance manual for testing in non-standard conditions.

q: How do you warm this engine up?
a: POH 4.17: warm up at 800 to 1200 RPM for not more than two minutes, and the handbook warns that prolonged idling at low RPM may result in fouled spark plugs. On start, when the engine is firing evenly the throttle is advanced to 800 RPM. The warm-up is not run to a temperature; it is run until the engine passes the throttle test in the ground check.

q: How do you know the engine is warm enough for takeoff?
a: It is a functional test, not a temperature. POH 4.19 and the GROUND CHECK list: the engine is warm for takeoff when the throttle can be opened without the engine faltering. That is a better answer than guessing an oil temperature, because the handbook sets no takeoff minimum; it publishes only the oil temperature green arc of 75 to 245 degrees F and the 245 degrees F red line.

q: The engine runs rough in cruise. Walk me through the checklist.
a: POH 3.3: carburetor heat ON; if roughness continues after one minute, carburetor heat OFF; mixture adjust for maximum smoothness; electric fuel pump ON; fuel selector switch tanks; engine gauges check; magneto switch L then R then BOTH; if operation is satisfactory on either one, continue on that magneto at reduced power and full rich mixture to the first airport; and prepare for a power-off landing. It works induction, then fuel, then ignition.

q: Is there anything special about shutting down after using alternate fuel?
a: Yes, and it is in the NOTE to POH 4.33: when alternate fuels are used, the engine should be run up to 1200 RPM for one minute prior to shutdown to clean out any unburned fuel. Alternate fuel here means the commercial grade 100/130 that 8.21 allows when 100 or 100LL is not available. The rest of the shutdown is mixture to idle cut-off with the throttle full aft, then magnetos and master off.

q: What type of oil system does this engine have?
a: A wet sump pressure system: the sump is an integral part of the engine, so oil falls back into it and is picked up again by the engine-driven pressure pump, rather than being held in a separate tank and scavenged as in a dry sump. I attribute that to the engine type, because this handbook never uses the phrase wet sump; what it gives is an 8 quart engine oil capacity, a dipstick and an oil cooler, which are all wet sump features.
