q: What is the oil capacity of this engine?
a: 8 US quarts. POH 1.9 prints oil capacity 8 quarts and 8.19 opens with the oil capacity of the engine is 8 quarts. TCDS 2A13 agrees independently: oil capacity 8 quarts at plus 27.5 inches, 6 quarts usable. Note those are two different ideas, capacity and usable oil, and an examiner may well ask you to separate them.

q: What is the minimum oil quantity for flight, and what are the other numbers people quote?
a: The POH figure is 2 quarts: Section 8.19, first sentence, the oil capacity of the engine is 8 quarts, and the minimum safe quantity is 2 quarts. The other two numbers are different things. The TCDS 6 quarts is usable oil, a weight and balance figure. A 6 to 8 quart band is a school dispatch policy, not a certification limit. I would fly to the school minimum, not to 2 quarts.
dup: How much oil must be in the engine before flight?

q: The type certificate says 6 quarts usable. Is that your minimum for flight?
a: No. 6 quarts usable is a weight and balance figure from TCDS 2A13, which reads oil capacity 8 quarts at plus 27.5, 6 quarts usable; it says how much of the oil is drainable and counted for loading, not how little you may dispatch with. The POH minimum safe quantity is 2 quarts, in Section 8.19. Mixing the two up is an easy way to get a follow-up question you do not want.

q: Why do some checklists say 6 to 8 quarts if the POH says 2?
a: Because that is an operator policy, not a handbook figure. One school's PA-28-161 checklist prints oil quantity 6 to 8 quarts as its preflight acceptance band, which is a sensible dispatch rule for an engine that uses oil on a long flight. The POH's own figure is the 2 quart minimum safe quantity in 8.19. The good answer names all three figures and says which is which.

q: Where is the oil cooler, and how is it cooled?
a: POH 7.5: the oil cooler is located on the left rear of the engine, mounted to the engine baffling, and the engine cooling air picked up in the nose section of the cowling and carried through the baffling is used on the left side for the oil cooler. There is no separate scoop for it; the same baffled air that cools the cylinders cools the oil.

q: What is the oil cooler winterization plate, and what is the rule for it?
a: POH 7.5: a winterization plate is provided to restrict air during winter operation. The placard in Section 2.25 gives the rule: oil cooler winterization plate to be removed when ambient temperature exceeds 50 degrees F. For a late November ride I would look for it on the preflight, know whether it is fitted, and know that I have to take it off once the temperature goes above that figure.

q: Is there a thermostatic bypass in the oil system, and how does it work?
a: There is one on the engine, but this handbook does not describe it. The words thermostat, bypass and vernatherm do not appear in the oil discussion; 7.5 covers the cooler and the winterization plate and 8.19 covers quantity, interval and grade. So the POH answer is the cooler and the plate, and I would say the thermostatic control of flow through the cooler is an engine-level detail I would confirm in the Lycoming manual rather than guess at the plumbing.

q: Is there an oil filter or a screen on this engine?
a: POH 8.19 names a full flow cartridge type oil filter and says it should be replaced each 50 hours of operation. The handbook does not describe a screen-only configuration, but it also does not state that every airframe has the filter, so which is actually fitted comes from the engine logbook and the accessory housing. It matters because it decides whether Lycoming's 50 hour or 25 hour interval applies.

q: How often is the oil changed on this airplane?
a: POH 8.19: the oil should be drained and renewed every 50 hours, and sooner under unfavorable operating conditions, with full flow cartridge type oil filters replaced each 50 hours as well. The full answer pairs that with the calendar limit on the same page: the interval between oil and oil filter change is not to exceed four months, whichever comes first.

q: Is there a calendar limit on the oil change as well as an hours limit?
a: Yes. POH 8.19: the interval between oil and oil filter change is not to exceed four months. So a training airplane hits the 50 hours first and a lightly flown private airplane hits the four months first. Quoting both is what makes the answer complete, because an airplane that has flown 20 hours in six months is still out of limits.

q: Lycoming talks about a 25 hour oil change. Where does that come from?
a: From Lycoming Service Bulletin 480, not from this handbook. It sets 25 hours with screen cleaning for an engine with a pressure screen system only, against 50 hours where there is a full flow filter, with four months either way. POH 8.19 publishes only the 50 hour and four month figures, so I would offer the 25 hour qualifier as Lycoming's and say it applies if the airplane turns out to have a screen rather than a filter.

q: What oil does this engine take?
a: The handbook deliberately does not freeze a brand. POH 1.9 and the NOTE at the end of 8.19 both refer the pilot to the latest issue of Lycoming Service Instruction 1014, Lubricating Oil Recommendations. What the POH does print is a viscosity table by average ambient temperature, with straight mineral grades under MIL-L-6082B in one column and ashless dispersant grades under MIL-L-22851 in the other.

q: It is a cold November morning. What oil grade should be in the engine?
a: The relevant row of the POH 8.19 table is 0 to 70 degrees F, which gives SAE 30 straight mineral, or 30, 40 or 20W-40 ashless dispersant. The all-temperature row allows 15W-50 or 20W-50 ashless dispersant, which is what most operators run year round. If the temperature ranges overlap, the table's own rule is to use the lighter grade oil.

q: What oil grade covers all temperatures?
a: The top row of the POH 8.19 table: 15W-50 or 20W-50 ashless dispersant under MIL-L-22851. The straight mineral column for that row is a dash, meaning no single grade mineral oil is recommended for all temperatures, which is the whole point of a multigrade. That row is why most Warriors on a flight line are on a 20W-50 all year.

q: What oil grade does the handbook call for in hot weather?
a: From the POH 8.19 table: above 80 degrees F, SAE 60 in either column; above 60 degrees F, SAE 50 straight mineral or 40 or 50 ashless dispersant; and 30 to 90 degrees F, SAE 40 in both columns. The rule printed with the table is that when operating temperatures overlap the indicated ranges, use the lighter grade oil.

q: What does the handbook call for below 10 degrees F?
a: The bottom row of the POH 8.19 table: SAE 20 straight mineral under MIL-L-6082B, or 30 or 20W-30 ashless dispersant under MIL-L-22851. In practice the all-temperature multigrade row, 15W-50 or 20W-50, covers that case too. A thinner oil in cold weather is about getting pressure and flow at start, before the engine has warmed.

q: The oil tables in Section 1 and Section 8 do not agree. Which one wins?
a: They really do differ, and spotting it is worth more than reciting either. Section 1.9 prints a shorter starting-viscosity table with no all-temperature row and gives 20W-30 below 10 degrees F, where 8.19 gives 30 or 20W-30. Section 8.19 is the servicing table and is the one I would quote, and I would say plainly that the handbook disagrees with itself and that Lycoming SI 1014 is the tie-breaker both sections point to.

q: What is break-in oil, and does this handbook require it?
a: This handbook says nothing about break-in oil. Section 8.19 refers the pilot to Lycoming Service Instruction 1014, and that document calls for non-dispersant mineral oil for the first 50 hours and after cylinder replacement until oil consumption stabilizes, for engines other than the O-320-H and O/LO-360-E series, so it does apply to this D-series engine. I would attribute the requirement to Lycoming, not to the POH.

q: What does the POH say about the dipstick?
a: Very little, and the honest answer says so. POH 4.13, nose section of the walk-around: check the oil level, and make sure that the dipstick has been properly seated. The handbook does not describe the filler neck, the access door or the dipstick markings, so I would not describe a calibrated scale from memory; I would read the stick in the airplane and compare it with the 8 quart capacity and the school minimum.

q: Describe the crankcase breather on this engine.
a: The handbook does not describe one. There is no mention of a crankcase breather or its routing anywhere in VB-1180. A breather does exist on the engine, venting blow-by and keeping crankcase pressure down, with the line routed so that it cannot freeze shut in cold weather, but that is engine manual material. I would say so rather than invent a routing, which is the same answer I would give for the thermostatic bypass.

q: What is the oil actually doing in the engine?
a: Lubrication first, and then cooling, sealing between the rings and the cylinder walls, cleaning by carrying combustion byproducts and metal to the filter, protecting against corrosion, and cushioning the bearings and gears. On this engine the cooling job is substantial because there are no cowl flaps and the oil cooler shares the baffled cylinder air, so high oil temperature in a climb is managed the same way as cylinder temperature.

q: What is the oil pressure green arc on this airplane?
a: POH 2.9: green arc, normal operating range, 60 to 90 PSI. That is the band you want in cruise. The gauge also carries two yellow arcs and two red lines, which is unusual and is a favorite examiner question, so it is worth being able to give all six numbers rather than only the green arc.

q: How many yellow arcs are on the oil pressure gauge, and what are they?
a: Two, which catches people out. POH 2.9: a yellow caution arc at idle from 25 to 60 PSI, and a second yellow arc for ground warm-up from 90 to 100 PSI. So low pressure at idle and high pressure on a cold morning run-up are both expected, caution-range indications rather than failures, as long as they move into the 60 to 90 green band with warm oil at normal power.

q: What are the red lines on the oil pressure gauge?
a: POH 2.7 and 2.9 agree: minimum red line 25 PSI and maximum red line 100 PSI. Below 25 PSI the engine is outside its limit and the answer is the loss of oil pressure procedure; above 100 PSI it is also out of limits, which is usually cold, thick oil or a regulating fault. Between them sit the two yellow arcs and the 60 to 90 PSI green arc.

q: What are the oil temperature markings?
a: POH 2.9: green arc, normal operating range, 75 to 245 degrees F, with the red line at 245 degrees F. The same 245 degrees F appears in 2.7 as the maximum oil temperature limitation, so the limit and the red line agree. There is no yellow arc on this gauge, so the answer is simply green to 245 and red at 245.

q: You get a low oil pressure light in flight. What does it actually tell you?
a: That a system may not be operating properly and that I should look at the gauge. POH 7.15 is explicit that the annunciator lights are provided only as a warning that he should check and monitor the applicable system gauge to determine when or if any necessary action is required. So the light sends me to the oil pressure and oil temperature gauges, and what those show decides whether this is a gauge problem or an engine problem.

q: You lose oil pressure in flight. What do you do?
a: The checklist is two lines, POH 3.3: land as soon as possible and investigate the cause, and prepare for a power-off landing. The amplified text at 3.17 is the part worth knowing: a partial loss usually indicates a malfunction in the oil pressure regulating system; a complete loss may signify oil exhaustion or a faulty gauge, and the engine may stop suddenly. Maintain altitude, and do not change power settings unnecessarily as that may hasten complete power loss.
dup: What does low oil pressure with rising oil temperature mean, and what do you do?

q: How do you tell a failed oil pressure gauge from a real loss of oil?
a: By what the other indications do. POH 3.17 says a complete loss of indication may signify oil exhaustion or may be the result of a faulty gauge, and that it may be advisable to make an off-airport landing while power is still available, particularly if other indications of actual oil pressure loss, such as sudden increases in temperatures, or oil smoke, are apparent, and an airport is not close. Rising oil temperature or smoke makes it real.

q: What is the procedure for high oil temperature?
a: POH 3.3, again only two lines: land at the nearest airport and investigate the problem, and prepare for a power-off landing. With no cowl flaps the only things that help on the way there are lowering the nose for more cooling airflow, reducing power, and enriching the mixture. If the pressure falls as the temperature rises, treat it as an impending engine failure and plan the landing accordingly.

q: Where are the oil gauges on the panel?
a: POH 7.19: in an engine cluster to the right of the pilot control wheel, which contains a fuel pressure gauge, a right and a left main fuel quantity gauge, an oil temperature gauge and an oil pressure gauge. Four of the gauges you are likely to be asked about are in that one cluster, with the tachometer, ammeter and annunciator panel elsewhere on the panel.

q: What is the oil arm, and when would you use it?
a: TCDS 2A13 gives oil capacity 8 quarts at plus 27.5 inches aft of datum, with 6 quarts usable. It is a weight and balance number for an airplane weighed with the oil drained. The Section 6 loading form in the POH does not list oil separately, because it treats the oil as part of the basic empty weight, so in normal loading I do not enter it at all.

q: How much fuel does this airplane hold?
a: 50 US gallons total, 48 usable, in two 25 gallon wing tanks of which 24 gallons a side is usable. POH 7.13 puts it in one sentence: fuel is stored in two twenty-five gallon tanks giving the airplane a total capacity of fifty U.S. gallons, 48 gallons usable. Sections 1.7 and 2.21 and TCDS 2A13 all agree, and I plan with 48, never 50.

q: What is the difference between total, usable and unusable fuel here?
a: Total is what the tanks hold, 50 gallons; usable is what the engine can actually draw in flight, 48 gallons, 24 a side; unusable is the 2 gallons that stays behind. POH 2.21 defines it exactly: the unusable fuel has been determined as 1.0 gallon in each wing in critical flight attitude. The unusable is already excluded from the 48 and is carried in the empty weight, and it never counts toward a reserve.
dup: What is the difference between total, usable and unusable fuel?

q: Why does the handbook define unusable fuel at the critical flight attitude?
a: Because fuel moves. POH 2.21: the unusable fuel has been determined as 1.0 gallon in each wing in critical flight attitude, not in level flight. The figure is set in the attitude where the outlet is most likely to be uncovered, so it is a conservative number. It is also why Operating Tip 10.3(i) warns about prolonged slips and skids uncovering the fuel outlet when the tank in use is not full.

q: What is the indicator tab in the filler neck, and how much fuel is it?
a: POH 7.13: each tank is equipped with a filler neck indicator tab to aid in determining fuel remaining when the tanks are not full, and the usable capacity to the bottom of the indicator tab is 17 gallons. So tabs is 17 a side, 34 gallons usable in total. On a weight-limited airplane that is how you fuel for a flight with four seats filled, instead of filling to the caps and leaving people behind.

q: What are the fuel selector positions?
a: Three: left tank, right tank and off. The selector face in Figure 7-7 is placarded L TANK 24 GAL, R TANK 24 GAL and FUEL OFF. The handle is on the left side panel forward of the pilot's seat. The point an examiner is usually driving at is the one that is not there, because this airplane has no BOTH position.

q: Does this airplane have a BOTH position on the fuel selector?
a: No. There are three positions only, left tank, right tank and off, confirmed on the Figure 7-7 selector face which is placarded L TANK 24 GAL, R TANK 24 GAL and FUEL OFF. So fuel management is an active job: run one tank, switch with the electric pump on, keep track of the time on each, and manage the lateral balance yourself.

q: Why is there no BOTH on a low-wing Piper?
a: The handbook gives no rationale, so I would separate the mechanism from my own reasoning. The sourced part is the arrangement: the tanks are in the wings below the engine, so there is no gravity feed and fuel is drawn up by an engine-driven pump with an electric pump as backup. Drawing both tanks through one suction line invites unporting and uneven feeding, so Piper selects one tank at a time and makes the pilot manage balance.

q: Where is the fuel selector and how do you get it to OFF?
a: POH 7.13: the selector is on the left side panel forward of the pilot's seat, and a button on the selector cover must be depressed and held while the handle is moved to the OFF position; the button releases automatically when the handle is moved back to ON. It is a guard against selecting OFF by accident in flight, and it is worth being able to find and work by feel.

q: What is the auxiliary electric fuel pump for?
a: POH 7.13: an auxiliary electric fuel pump is provided in case of the failure of the engine-driven pump. Note what that does not say. It is not the normal supply and it is not a primer; it is a backup that is switched on for the phases where an engine-driven pump failure would be least survivable. The switch is in the switch panel above the throttle quadrant.

q: When is the electric fuel pump on?
a: The sentence is POH 7.13: the electric pump should be ON for all takeoffs and landings and when switching tanks. It is reinforced three more times in the same book: electric fuel pump on appears on the placarded takeoff checklist and the placarded landing checklist, and again in the Before Takeoff and Landing lists in Section 4. In the climb it comes off at the desired altitude.
dup: When do you use the auxiliary or boost fuel pump?

q: Why do you turn the electric fuel pump off during the run-up?
a: POH 4.19 gives the reason outright: the electric fuel pump should be turned OFF after starting or during warm-up to make sure that the engine driven pump is operating. It is a functional check of the engine-driven pump, which is why the GROUND CHECK list has electric fuel pump OFF followed immediately by fuel pressure check. Prior to takeoff it goes on again to prevent loss of power during takeoff should the engine-driven pump fail.

q: When does the electric fuel pump come off after takeoff?
a: The Section 4 CLIMB checklist says OFF at desired altitude, not at a fixed height above the ground. The logic is the same as turning it on: it is there so an engine-driven pump failure in a critical phase does not become a power loss, so it stays on until the airplane is somewhere a power loss could be handled. It goes back on for the approach and landing.

q: Is there a fuel emergency where the electric pump goes off rather than on?
a: Yes, and it is the trap. Both engine fire checklists turn the electric fuel pump OFF, with the fuel selector OFF as well: engine fire during start is starter crank, mixture idle cut-off, throttle open, electric fuel pump OFF, fuel selector OFF; engine fire in flight is fuel selector OFF, throttle closed, mixture idle cut-off, electric fuel pump check OFF. Every other fuel emergency turns it on.

q: Where is the engine-driven fuel pump in the system?
a: POH 7.5 lists a fuel pump among the engine-driven accessories, and the Figure 7-9 schematic shows it labeled ENGINE FUEL PUMP in the line between the strainer and the carburetor, with the electric pump upstream of it. In normal operation it is the pump doing the work; the electric pump sits in parallel as the backup, which is why switching the electric one off in the run-up proves the engine-driven one is alive.

q: Trace the fuel from the tank to the cylinders.
a: From Figure 7-9: left or right main tank, then the fuel tank selector valve, then the fuel strainer, then the electric fuel pump, then the engine fuel pump, then the carburetor and on into the induction system. The primer taps off the line between the strainer and the carburetor, the fuel pressure gauge reads at the carburetor, and the quantity gauges read the tanks.

q: What does the handbook call the gascolator, and where is it?
a: It calls it the fuel strainer, and I would use the handbook's word. POH 7.13: a fuel strainer, located on the lower left front of the fire wall, has a drain which is accessible from outside the nose section. Section 8.21 puts the quick drain on the front lower corner of the fire wall, and the walk-around says to open the fuel strainer located on the left side of the fire wall.

q: How many fuel screens are there, and how often are they cleaned?
a: Three, and that detail scores. POH 8.21: at every 50-hour inspection, the fuel screens in the strainer, in the electric fuel pump, and at the carburetor inlet must be cleaned. Most candidates know only the strainer. The strainer itself is the one the pilot touches, through the quick drain on the front lower corner of the fire wall.

q: How many fuel drains does this airplane have, and where are they?
a: Three drain points. POH 8.21: each fuel tank is equipped with an individual quick drain located at the lower inboard rear corner of the tank, and the fuel strainer is equipped with a quick drain located on the front lower corner of the fire wall. So that is one per wing tank plus the strainer. I would still count them on the airplane, because the walk-around text uses the plural for the tank sumps.

q: What is the correct order for draining the fuel system?
a: POH 8.21: each of the fuel tank sumps should be drained first, then the fuel strainer should be drained twice, once with the fuel selector valve on each tank. Each time, enough fuel should be allowed to flow to ensure removal of contaminants, collected in a suitable container, examined for contaminants and proper fuel, then discarded. Most candidates drain the strainer once; doing it on each tank selection is the scoring detail.

q: When does the handbook require the fuel system to be drained?
a: POH 8.21: the fuel system sumps and strainer should be drained daily prior to the first flight and after refueling, to avoid the accumulation of contaminants such as water or sediment and to check for proper fuel. Section 7.13 says the same: the fuel drains should be opened daily prior to first flight, and the strainer should also be drained before the first flight of the day.

q: Why do you drain fuel samples, and what are you looking for?
a: Water, sediment and the wrong fuel. The POH's phrase is contaminants such as water or sediment, and proper fuel, so the sample is checked for the blue color of 100LL, for the smell of avgas rather than kerosene, and for water, which sits as clear beads or a separate layer in the bottom because it is denser than fuel. Water gets in from condensation, rain past a bad cap and from the truck.
dup: Why do you drain fuel samples, and what are you looking for?

q: What cautions does the handbook attach to draining fuel?
a: Three, all in POH 8.21. When draining any amount of fuel, care should be taken to ensure that no fire hazard exists before starting the engine; after draining, each quick drain should be checked to make sure it has closed completely and is not leaking; and fuel additive cannot be used as a substitute for preflight draining of the fuel system drains. The leaking drain is the one that catches people out after a cold morning sample.

q: Is a fuel anti-icing additive approved on this airplane?
a: Yes, with limits. POH 8.21: the additive must meet specification MIL-I-27686 and be uniformly blended with the fuel while refueling, not exceeding .15 percent by volume and not less than .10 percent, which is about one and one half liquid ounces per ten gallons. The CAUTION on the same page is the part to remember: fuel additive cannot be used as a substitute for preflight draining of the fuel system drains.

q: Tell me about the fuel tank vents.
a: The walk-around checks one per wing: POH 4.13 says the fuel tank vent should be clear of obstructions on both the right and the left wing. Section 7 does not describe the vents at all, so I would not invent a type or a location beyond that. The purpose is standard reasoning: the vent keeps the space above the fuel at ambient pressure as fuel is drawn off, so no vacuum can build and starve the engine.

q: Where are the fuel quantity gauges, and what powers them?
a: POH 7.13: the fuel quantity and fuel pressure gauges are mounted in a gauge cluster on the left side of the instrument panel to the right of the control wheel, a right and a left main gauge. They are electrically powered, because 7.15 lists the fuel gauge among the standard electrical accessories. That matters directly to the alternator failure answer: as the battery runs down, the fuel gauges are among the things you lose.

q: Are the fuel gauges only accurate at empty?
a: That claim is not in this handbook. It comes from the certification rule, not from Piper, and the full text of VB-1180 makes no statement about gauge accuracy. What the POH does require is better: at 4.13 it has you open the fuel cap on each wing, visually check the fuel color, and confirm the quantity matches the indication on the gauge. So fuel is planned by known quantity and time, with the gauge as the cross-check.

q: What is the minimum fuel grade for this airplane?
a: POH 2.7: AVGAS ONLY, minimum grade 100 or 100LL aviation grade, and the filler placard reads FUEL 100 OR 100LL AVIATION GRADE. Section 8.21 puts it more bluntly: the minimum aviation grade fuel for the PA-28-161 is 100, and since the use of lower grades can cause serious engine damage in a short period of time, the engine warranty is invalidated by the use of lower octanes.

q: What are the aviation fuel grades and their colors?
a: From POH 1.7 and the Section 8 fuel grade comparison chart: current grades are 80 red, 100LL blue and 100 green; previous grades were 80/87 red, 91/96 blue, 100/130 green and 115/145 purple. There is a footnote worth knowing: grade 100LL in some overseas countries is colored green and designated 100L. The color check on the preflight is how you catch a misfueling.
dup: What are the aviation fuel grades and their colors?

q: You land somewhere with no 100LL. What can you put in it?
a: POH 8.21: whenever 100 or 100LL grade fuel is not available, commercial grade 100/130 should be used, and the handbook refers to Lycoming Service Instruction 1070. Lower grades are not an option; the same paragraph says their use can cause serious engine damage in a short period and invalidates the engine warranty. If I use the alternate fuel, 4.33 wants 1200 RPM for one minute before shutdown to clean out unburned fuel.

q: What would happen if this airplane were fueled with jet fuel?
a: It would not run on it. The airplane is placarded AVGAS ONLY, minimum grade 100, and jet fuel is kerosene, which is not an approved grade at all. In a spark-ignition engine with an 8.5:1 compression ratio it will not burn properly, giving severe detonation, roughness and power loss, usually shortly after takeoff. The defenses are the placard at the filler, watching the truck, and the handbook's own requirement to open the cap and check the fuel color at every preflight.

q: What is the difference between fuel starvation and fuel exhaustion?
a: Exhaustion is no fuel left on board; starvation is fuel on board that is not reaching the engine, typically the selector on a tank that is dry while the other is full. Starvation is the one with a cure in the air: the first line of the engine power loss checklist is fuel selector switch to a tank containing fuel. POH 3.9 warns that the engine will not restart instantly, because the empty lines have to fill, which may require up to ten seconds.

q: How long can this airplane fly on its fuel?
a: That has to come from the airplane's own performance section, but the structure of the answer is fixed: start from 48 gallons usable rather than the 50 gallon total, take off the regulatory reserve for the kind of flight, and divide what is left by the planned fuel flow at the chosen power setting. The cruise charts in the handbook I have are computed for a heavier airplane, so the fuel flow figures themselves must come from this airplane's own book.

q: Does slipping this airplane have any fuel implication?
a: Yes, and it is in the Warrior's own Operating Tips at 10.3(i): prolonged slips or skids which result in excess of 2000 ft of altitude loss, or other radical or extreme maneuvers which could cause uncovering of the fuel outlet, must be avoided, as fuel flow interruption may occur when the tank being used is not full. That matters directly to steep spirals and to slipping off height on a power-off landing.

q: What do the fuel pressure markings on the gauge mean?
a: POH 2.9: green arc, normal operating range, 0.5 to 8 PSI, with the red line minimum at 0.5 PSI and the red line maximum at 8 PSI. Note that the minimum is half a PSI, not 5; the OCR of the handbook mangles it but the printed page reads .5. Those same two figures appear as power plant limitations in 2.7.

q: You lose fuel pressure in flight. What is the drill?
a: The checklist is two lines, POH 3.3: electric fuel pump ON, and fuel selector check on a full tank. That is the whole published procedure, and it makes sense because the two likely causes are an engine-driven pump failure, which the electric pump covers, and a selector on a tank that has run dry. If pressure and power do not come back, the next step is the engine power loss checklist and a power-off landing.

q: The engine coughs and the fuel pressure stays normal. What does that suggest?
a: Water. POH 3.11 makes the point directly: if power loss is due to water, fuel pressure indications will be normal, because the pump is delivering liquid, just not fuel. The handbook's advice is to allow the engine to windmill, and if the engine does not restart after a reasonable time, to try switching tanks. It is also the argument for draining the sumps and the strainer properly before the first flight of the day.

q: Which fuel filler placard belongs on this airplane?
a: The plain one: FUEL - 100 OR 100LL AVIATION GRADE. The handbook prints a second, graphic AVGAS ONLY placard with GRADE 100LL and GRADE 100, but Section 2.25 restricts that version to serial numbers 28-8316037 and up. This airplane is 28-8116257, well below that, so it gets the first one. The handbook does the serial reasoning for you there, which is a cheap way to show you understand applicability.

q: Describe this airplane's electrical system in one sentence.
a: POH 7.15: the electrical system includes a 14-volt, 60-amp alternator, a 12-volt battery, a voltage regulator, an overvoltage relay and a master switch relay. The distinction an examiner may probe is in that sentence: it is a 14 volt charging system supplying a 12 volt battery, because the charging voltage has to sit above the battery's resting voltage for current to flow into it.

q: What is the alternator rated at, and how is it driven?
a: 60 amps at 14 volts, given in two places, POH 7.15 and 7.5. The handbook never states the drive in 7.5 or 7.15, but the walk-around at 4.13 says to check the alternator belt for proper tension in the nose section, so it is belt driven off the engine. The advantage over a generator worth stating is that an alternator gives useful output at low engine RPM, including on the ground at idle.

q: Where is the battery on this airplane?
a: On this serial it is aft of the main spar, not on the firewall. VB-880, the handbook that applies to serials 28-7716001 through 28-8216300, says the battery is mounted in a thermoplastic box immediately aft of the main spar. The widely circulated VB-1180 handbook puts it on the forward right face of the fire wall, because Piper moved it between the serial blocks. I would open the airplane and look before answering in the oral.

q: Why does it matter where the battery is?
a: Because the consequences differ. Aft of the main spar it is a weight and balance item behind the center of gravity, under the rear seat area, and it is not reachable in flight; on the firewall it is in the engine compartment under the right cowl, where the servicing instructions in 8.25 about raising the upper right cowl would apply. The online handbook for this model gives the firewall answer, and for this serial that is the wrong one.

q: What is the battery's capacity in amp hours?
a: The handbook does not give one. VB-1180 prints the voltage only, 12 volts, and no amp-hour rating appears anywhere in it, so I would read the battery label or the equipment list rather than quote a figure. Warriors fly with both 25 and 35 amp hour batteries in service. The same gap means the handbook publishes no battery endurance after an alternator failure either.

q: What type of battery is it, and how is it serviced?
a: The handbook never names the chemistry, but 8.25 describes servicing that only fits a flooded lead-acid cell: the battery should be checked for proper fluid level, do not fill above the baffle plates, do not fill with acid, use only water, and a hydrometer check will determine the percent of charge. A sealed battery may have been fitted since, so that is something to confirm on the airplane.

q: How is the battery recharged, per the handbook?
a: POH 8.25: if the battery is not up to charge, recharge starting at a 4 amp rate and finishing with a 2 amp rate, and quick charges are not recommended. The same section says the battery box has a drain tube, normally closed off with a cap, which should be opened occasionally to drain off any accumulation of liquid, although that description belongs to the firewall installation.

q: Is the master switch a single switch?
a: No, it is split into BAT and ALT halves. The handbook does not describe the switch itself, but the Section 3 procedures operate the halves independently and in opposition, which only a split switch allows. Some airframes have the ALT half mechanically interlocked with the BAT half, so it is worth trying to move ALT alone on the ground to see which this one is.

q: Justify the split master switch from the handbook alone.
a: From the two Section 3 procedures. ELECTRICAL FAILURES turns the ALT switch OFF while the battery stays on, sheds load, checks and resets the ALT breaker and then puts ALT back on. ELECTRICAL OVERLOAD does the opposite, ALT switch ON and BATT switch OFF, to shed a runaway regulator while keeping the alternator feeding the airplane. You cannot fly either checklist with a single-pole master, so the book justifies the switch.

q: What does the ammeter in this airplane tell you?
a: POH 7.15, in its own words: unlike previous generator systems, the ammeter as installed does not show battery discharge; rather, it indicates the electrical load on the alternator in amperes. It is a loadmeter. If I answered that it shows whether the battery is charging or discharging, I would have described a different airplane, and everything else I said about the electrical system would get re-examined.
dup: What is the ammeter or loadmeter telling you?

q: So the ammeter never shows a discharge?
a: Correct, it reads load, not charge or discharge. POH 7.15 says the ammeter as installed does not show battery discharge; it indicates the electrical load on the alternator in amperes. There is no negative side to the scale to swing into. That is exactly why alternator failure shows as a zero reading rather than a discharge, which is the indication the Section 3 checklist tells you to look for.

q: What should the ammeter read on a normal night flight?
a: POH 7.15 gives the example: the average continuous load for night flight with radios on is about 30 amperes, and this 30 ampere value plus approximately 2 amperes for a fully charged battery will appear continuously under these flight conditions. So a steady reading in the low thirties on a night flight is the system working, not a problem, and on a 60 amp alternator that is comfortable.

q: What does the ammeter read with everything off and the master on?
a: POH 7.15: with all the electrical equipment off and the master switch on, the ammeter will indicate the charging rate of the battery, and as each electrical unit is switched on it will indicate the total ampere draw of all the units including the battery. So the needle climbs as you add load, and with a fully charged battery and nothing on it sits at only a couple of amperes.

q: How do you confirm from the ammeter that the alternator is working?
a: By comparing the needle with what you have switched on. POH 7.15: the amount of current shown on the ammeter will tell immediately if the alternator system is operating normally, as the amount of current shown should equal the total amperage drawn by the electrical equipment which is operating. If I switch on the landing light and the pitot heat and the reading does not move, the alternator is not carrying the load.

q: What does a zero reading on the ammeter mean?
a: Alternator failure. POH 3.23 says it flatly: loss of alternator output is detected through zero reading on the ammeter, and the Section 3 checklist is written as if ammeter shows zero. That indication is itself proof the gauge is a loadmeter, because a center-zero charge and discharge ammeter would swing to discharge instead. Everything on the airplane is then running off the battery alone.

q: The handbook calls the same instrument three things. What are they?
a: Ammeter in Section 7.15 and in the Section 3 procedures, volt-ammeter in the 2.19 Day VFR required equipment list, and alternator gauge on the Figure 7-15 instrument panel layout. They are the same gauge. The one to keep in mind for a legality question is the required equipment list, because a volt-ammeter is one of the twelve items the handbook requires for day VFR in this airplane.

q: Where are the voltage regulator and overvoltage relay?
a: POH 7.15: the regulator and overvoltage relay are located on the forward left side of the fuselage behind the instrument panel. The regulator holds system voltage steady as engine speed and load change, and the overvoltage relay takes the alternator off line if the regulator runs away, which protects the radios and the battery from an overvoltage condition.

q: What is the overvoltage relay, and can you reset it in flight?
a: It takes the alternator off line if the regulator fails high, and yes, cycling the ALT switch is the reset. POH 3.23: if the alternator failure was caused by a momentary overvoltage condition, 16.5 volts and up, that procedure should return the system to normal. That is why the ELECTRICAL FAILURES checklist turns the ALT switch off, sheds load, checks the breaker and then turns ALT back on before giving up on it.

q: What lights are on the annunciator panel?
a: POH 7.15: the annunciator panel includes alternator and low oil pressure indicator lights, and when the optional gyro system is installed it also includes a low vacuum indicator light. So three at most, and the third depends on whether this airplane has the vacuum system. Section 7.19 confirms the panel warns of a possible malfunction in the alternator, oil pressure or vacuum systems.

q: What does an annunciator light actually tell you?
a: Less than people think, and the handbook says so. POH 7.15: the annunciator panel lights are provided only as a warning to the pilot that a system may not be operating properly, and that he should check and monitor the applicable system gauge to determine when or if any necessary action is required. The light is a prompt to look at a gauge, not a diagnosis, and that is exactly how the Section 3 checklists are written.

q: The ALT light comes on in cruise with everything switched off. What now?
a: Add a little load and watch. POH 7.15, repeated as the first NOTE of the Section 3 ELECTRICAL FAILURES checklist: when operating with light electrical load and a fully charged battery, the Alternator Inop. light may illuminate due to minimal alternator output, and if the alternator is functional a slight increase in electrical load should extinguish the Inop. indication. If it stays on, I check the ammeter for zero and run the checklist.

q: How do you check the annunciator panel?
a: With the press-to-test button. It is on the Section 4 GROUND CHECK list as annunciator panel press-to-test, and 4.19 repeats it: check the annunciator panel lights with the press-to-test button. The lights are also checked on the cockpit preflight with the master on, where the walk-around has you confirm the panel illuminates before turning the master off again.

q: What is on the standard electrical accessory list?
a: POH 7.15: starter, electric fuel pump, stall warning indicator, cigar lighter, fuel gauge, ammeter and annunciator panel. That list is the direct answer to what you lose when the electrical system fails, and the two items on it that catch people out are the stall warning horn and the fuel quantity gauges. Just as important is what is not on the list, because the ignition is not.

q: What is on the optional electrical accessory list?
a: POH 7.15: navigation lights, wing tip recognition lights, anti-collision light, landing light, instrument lighting and cabin dome light, with the note that the circuits will handle the addition of communications and navigational equipment. Lighting being optional in the certification sense does not make it optional for a night flight, where 2.19 requires position lights, instrument lights and anti-collision lights.

q: Does this airplane use fuses or circuit breakers, and where are they?
a: Circuit breakers, on the lower right instrument panel, per POH 7.15 and Figure 7-13; no fuses are described anywhere in the handbook. Section 7.19 adds that the radios and the circuit breakers are on the upper and lower right panel respectively. The handbook's own airmanship on them is Operating Tip 10.3(d): before attempting to reset any circuit breaker, allow a two to five minute cooling off period.

q: A circuit breaker pops in flight. What do you do?
a: Decide first whether I need that circuit. If it is not needed, I leave it alone. If it is, Operating Tip 10.3(d) is the handbook's rule: before attempting to reset any circuit breaker, allow a two to five minute cooling off period. Then one reset only, and if it pops again I leave it out, because a breaker that trips twice is telling me there is a fault, and resetting into a fault is how an electrical fire starts.
dup: How do you handle a circuit breaker that has popped?

q: Is there an avionics bus on this airplane?
a: POH 7.19 describes one. An optional radio master switch near the top of the instrument panel between the radio stacks controls power to all radios through the aircraft master switch, and an emergency bus switch supplies auxiliary power to the avionics bus in the event of a radio master switch circuit failure. That switch is behind the lower right shin guard, left of the circuit breaker panel, and the radio master is optional, so I would confirm what is actually fitted.

q: Does this airplane have an external power receptacle?
a: Piper External Power is listed as optional in POH 7.33, through a receptacle on the right side of the fuselage forward of the wing, which lets an external battery crank the engine without getting at the airplane's own battery. The Section 4 procedure is master off and all electrical equipment off, connect the terminals, insert the plug, start normally, disconnect the plug, then master switch on and check the ammeter.

q: The ALT light is on and the ammeter reads zero. Give me the checklist in order.
a: POH 3.3 ELECTRICAL FAILURES: ammeter check to verify the alternator is inoperative; if the ammeter shows zero, ALT switch OFF; reduce electrical loads to minimum; ALT circuit breaker check and reset as required; ALT switch ON. If power is not restored, ALT switch OFF, reduce electrical loads and land as soon as practical, because the battery is the only remaining source of electrical power. Note that load shedding comes before the breaker reset.

q: What is the amplified reasoning behind the alternator failure checklist?
a: POH 3.23: loss of alternator output is detected through zero reading on the ammeter; if no increase in the ammeter reading is noted, alternator failure can be confirmed; check the alternator circuit breakers for a popped circuit; then attempt to reset the overvoltage relay, which cures a momentary overvoltage condition of 16.5 volts and up. If the ammeter continues to indicate zero, or the alternator will not remain reset, turn the alternator off, keep the load to a minimum and land as soon as practical.

q: After an alternator failure, what keeps working?
a: The engine, because the magnetos are self-exciting and need no electrical power; the vacuum gyros, because 7.17 makes the vacuum pump engine driven; the flaps, because 7.9 makes them manual, a cable and a handle; and the brakes, which are hydraulic through the toe pedals and the hand lever. None of those four depends on the battery, which is why this failure is a workload problem rather than an emergency.

q: After an alternator failure, what do you lose as the battery runs down?
a: Everything on the standard electrical list and the options: the electric fuel pump, the stall warning horn, the fuel quantity gauges, the ammeter, the annunciator panel, the cigar lighter, all the lighting, the radios and transponder, and the turn indicator, which 7.19 says is the electrically operated one. The stall warning is the one candidates forget, and 4.37 states it: the stall warning system is inoperative with the master switch OFF.

q: How long will the battery last after an alternator failure?
a: The handbook publishes no figure, and I would not invent minutes. No amp-hour rating appears anywhere in it either, so there is nothing to divide. The useful answer is the procedure: reduce electrical loads to a minimum, keep what I need for the approach, and land as soon as practical, treating whatever is left as a reserve of unknown size rather than planning a leg on it.

q: What is an electrical overload, and how would you recognize it?
a: POH 3.24 defines it in its own heading: alternator output more than 20 amps above the known electrical load. So it is recognized on the ammeter, by the needle reading far more current than the equipment switched on can account for, which points at a regulator failing high and driving current into the battery. It is the one case where you fly with the alternator on and the battery off.

q: Give me the electrical overload checklist.
a: POH 3.3: ALT switch ON, BATT switch OFF. If alternator loads are reduced, reduce the electrical load to minimum and land as soon as practical, with the NOTE that due to increased system voltage and radio frequency noise, operation with ALT on and BATT off should be made only when required by an electrical system failure. If loads are not reduced, ALT switch OFF, BATT as required, land as soon as possible and anticipate complete electrical failure.

q: Why are there two different urgencies in the overload procedure?
a: Because the two outcomes are different problems. If turning the battery off reduces the alternator loads, the airplane is stable on alternator power and the handbook says land as soon as practical. If the loads do not reduce, the fault is not the battery and the handbook says land as soon as possible and anticipate complete electrical failure. Being able to explain why the wording changes is better than reciting the steps.

q: You have an electrical fire in flight. What happens to the airplane when you do the drill?
a: The drill is POH 3.3: master switch OFF, vents open, cabin heat off, land as soon as practical. On this airplane that means losing the electric fuel pump, the stall warning horn, the fuel gauges, the ammeter, the annunciator and the radios, while the engine keeps running on the magnetos and the vacuum gyros keep running off the engine-driven pump. Cabin heat goes off because its air comes off the muffler shroud.

q: What does the strobe light placard say, and why?
a: The placard in full view of the pilot reads: WARNING - TURN OFF STROBE LIGHTS WHEN IN CLOSE PROXIMITY TO GROUND OR DURING FLIGHT THROUGH CLOUD, FOG OR HAZE. The same warning appears in 7.15 and in Operating Tip 10.3(f). The reason is disorientation: the strobes reflect off cloud or fog and off the ground on the taxiway and can be blinding to the pilot and to others.

q: What switches should be off before you engage the starter, and why?
a: Operating Tip 10.3(e): check the radio, light and pitot heat switches off before engaging the starter, so as not to create an overloaded condition when the starter is engaged. The starter is the biggest single draw on the airplane, so everything else comes off first; it is also why the external power procedure has you start with the master and all electrical equipment off.

q: Describe this airplane in the handbook's own words.
a: POH 7.1: the Warrior II is a single-engine, fixed gear monoplane of all metal construction with low semi-tapered wings; it has four place seating and a baggage capacity of two hundred pounds. That one sentence answers a surprising number of questions, including why there is no gear emergency procedure anywhere in Section 3.

q: What airfoil does the wing use, and how is the wing attached?
a: POH 7.3: a NACA 652415 laminar flow, semi-tapered airfoil. The cantilever wings are attached to each side of the fuselage by inserting the butt ends of the main spars into a spar box carry-through located under the rear seat, which in effect gives a continuous main spar, plus an auxiliary front spar and a rear spar. The rear spar takes torque and drag loads and mounts the flaps and ailerons.

q: What is a stabilator, and what is the tab on its trailing edge?
a: A stabilator is a one-piece, all-moving horizontal tail: the whole surface pivots rather than a hinged elevator on a fixed stabilizer. POH 7.3 describes the tab in its own words: the stabilator incorporates an anti-servo tab which improves longitudinal stability and provides longitudinal trim; this tab moves in the same direction as the stabilator, but with increased travel.

q: Why does a stabilator need an anti-servo tab?
a: Because an all-moving surface is aerodynamically over-sensitive: the whole tail generates the force, so very little stick force is needed and the pilot can easily overcontrol it. The anti-servo tab deflects the same way as the stabilator but with increased travel, which pushes back against the pilot and raises the control force as deflection increases. POH 7.3 says it improves longitudinal stability and provides longitudinal trim.

q: How does an anti-servo tab differ from a servo or balance tab?
a: By which way it moves. A servo or balance tab deflects opposite to the surface to help the pilot move it and lighten the controls; an anti-servo tab deflects the same way as the surface, so it opposes the movement and increases the force the pilot feels. POH 7.3 states the same-direction movement explicitly, with increased travel, which is the half of the answer most candidates miss.

q: How could you demonstrate the anti-servo tab on the walk-around?
a: By moving the stabilator by hand and watching the tab. Push the stabilator trailing edge down and the tab goes down with it, not up, which is the whole distinction from a balance tab. The same check confirms the surface is free and that the tab linkage is connected, and 7.9 adds the handbook's other point about it: the tab serves the dual function of providing trim control and pitch control forces.

q: How is pitch trim arranged on this airplane?
a: Through the same anti-servo tab. POH 7.9: a trim control wheel on the control console between the front seats, where forward rotation gives nose down trim and aft rotation gives nose up trim. There is no separate trim tab, so the one surface both trims the airplane and supplies the pitch control forces, which is the dual function the handbook describes.

q: What kind of flaps does this airplane have?
a: POH 7.9: manually controlled flaps, extended by a control cable from a handle between the two front seats, balanced and spring loaded to return to the retracted position. Section 7.3 calls them four-position wing flaps. Because they are mechanical rather than electric, they are one of the systems you keep after an electrical failure, and because they are spring loaded you feel the airplane want them back up.

q: What flap settings are available, and how do you select them?
a: POH 7.9: the handle is pulled up to the desired flap setting of 10, 25 or 40 degrees, with retracted making the fourth position. To retract, depress the button on the end of the handle and lower the control. Section 4 refers to 25 degrees as the second notch, which is the setting used for a short field takeoff over an obstacle and for both soft field takeoffs.

q: What happens to pitch when you move the flaps?
a: POH 7.9: when extending or retracting flaps there is a pitch change in the airplane, and this pitch change can be corrected either by stabilator trim or by increased control wheel force. The handbook does not say which way, so I would fly it and trim it rather than recite a direction. It is also why the takeoff and landing checklists both have flaps set before the critical phase, not during it.

q: Why does Piper warn you about standing on the flap?
a: Because only one of them is a step and only in one position. POH 7.9: when the flaps are retracted the right flap, provided with an over-center lock mechanism, acts as a step, and the NOTE adds that the right flap will support a load only in the fully retracted position. The warning is repeated five times in the handbook, in 7.9, 4.33, 4.35, the preflight caution and Operating Tip 10.3(c), which tells you how often it was ignored.

q: Describe the landing gear.
a: POH 7.7: fixed tricycle gear with three air-oil struts, Cleveland 5.00 by 5 nose wheel and 6.00 by 6 main wheels, with four-ply tires of the same sizes. Normal static load extension is 3.25 inches on the nose strut and 4.50 inches on each main, and the walk-around gives both a plus or minus .25 inch tolerance. A shimmy dampener is included in the nose gear.

q: What are the tire pressures?
a: POH 8.23: 30 psi for the nose gear and 24 psi for the main gear. Section 7.7 gives the same two figures but qualifies them at gross weight. Section 8.23 adds that the wheels and tires are balanced before original installation and the relationship of tire, tube and wheel should be kept on reinstallation, and that unbalanced wheels can cause extreme vibration in the landing gear.

q: How is this airplane steered on the ground?
a: Through the nose wheel and the brakes. POH 7.7: the nose gear is steerable through a 30 degree arc each side of center using the rudder pedals and brakes, with a bungee in the mechanism to reduce steering effort and damp bumps; later aircraft have the bungee removed and are steerable through a 20 degree arc each side. The handbook never defines later aircraft, so for a 1981 airplane I would give both and say I would confirm which this one is.

q: Describe the brake system.
a: POH 7.7: Cleveland single disc hydraulic brakes on the main gear only, with no brake on the nose wheel. They are actuated either by toe brake pedals attached to the rudder pedals or by a hand lever and master cylinder located below and behind the center of the instrument sub panel, with hydraulic cylinders above each pedal and next to the hand lever. The fluid reservoir is on the top left front face of the fire wall.

q: How does the parking brake work?
a: POH 7.7: it is incorporated in the master cylinder, and it is set by pulling back on the brake lever and depressing the knob attached to the left side of the handle. To release it, pull back on the brake lever to disengage the catch mechanism and let the handle swing forward. Because it works through the same master cylinder as the hand brake, a leak that loses the brakes loses the parking brake too.

q: How much warning does the stall warning give, and what powers it?
a: POH 7.29 and 4.37: the indicator activates at between five and ten knots above stall speed, and the NOTE at 4.37 says the stall warning system is inoperative with the master switch OFF, because it is an electrical accessory. So in an electrical fire with the master off, or late in an alternator failure, the horn is gone and the only stall warning left is the airplane itself.

q: How do you check the stall warning on the preflight?
a: POH 4.13 and 4.37: turn the master switch ON, lift the detector and check that the horn sounds, then turn the master back off. That is the check the handbook gives. What it does not give is the mechanism, or which wing the detector is on; the lift detector on the left wing leading edge comes from the Piper maintenance manual rather than from this handbook, so I would attribute it rather than claim it as a POH fact.

q: Describe the pitot-static system on this airplane.
a: POH 7.21: pitot and static pressure are both picked up by a pitot head installed on the bottom of the left wing, and carried through pitot and static lines within the wing and fuselage to the gauges on the instrument panel. That is the detail people miss: there are no fuselage static ports at all. The system supplies the airspeed indicator, the altimeter and the optional vertical speed indicator.

q: Where are the static ports on this airplane?
a: There are none on the fuselage. POH 7.21 is explicit that pitot and static pressure are picked up by a single pitot head on the bottom of the left wing, so the static source is part of that combined head. The walk-around says to remove the cover from the pitot/static head on the underside of the wing and make sure the holes are open and clear. The static wicks on the wings are nothing to do with it.

q: What are the static wicks for?
a: They are precipitation static dischargers, there to bleed off static charge the airframe picks up in cloud and rain so it does not interfere with the radios. The walk-around checks them on both wings for firm attachment and good condition. They have nothing to do with the static system, which is an easy trap on this airplane precisely because it has no fuselage static ports to point at.

q: Does this airplane have an alternate static source?
a: It is optional. POH 7.21: an alternate static source is available as optional equipment, with the control valve located below the left side of the instrument panel. So the honest answer is that I would look under the left side of the panel in this airplane and confirm. If there is none, the fallback for a blocked static source is to break the glass of the vertical speed indicator, accepting the reversed VSI.

q: If the alternate static source is fitted, how do you use it?
a: POH 7.21: with the valve in the alternate position the altimeter, vertical speed indicator and airspeed indicator use cabin air for static pressure. The conditions are the scoring detail: the storm window and cabin vents must be closed and the cabin heater and defroster must be on during alternate static source operation, and the altimeter error is less than 50 feet unless otherwise placarded.

q: Does this airplane have pitot heat?
a: POH 7.21 lists a heated pitot head as optional equipment, which alleviates problems with icing and heavy rain, with the switch on the electrical switch panel to the left of the right control wheel. It is a substantial electrical load, so it is one of the first things to shed after an alternator failure, and Operating Tip 10.3(e) wants it off before engaging the starter.

q: Does this airplane have a vacuum system?
a: Section 7.17 is footnoted as optional equipment, and 7.19 lists the attitude gyro, directional gyro and suction gauge as panel options, so it has to be confirmed on this airplane. If it is there, 7.17 describes it: an engine driven vacuum pump, a vacuum regulator, a filter and the necessary plumbing. For IFR it is not optional at all, because POH 2.19 lists a vacuum pump and gyro suction indicator as day IFR equipment.

q: What does the vacuum system drive, and what is driven electrically?
a: POH 7.17 and 7.19: the attitude gyro and directional gyro are vacuum operated through a vacuum pump installed on the engine, while the turn and slip indicator is electrically operated. The split is deliberate: a single failure, vacuum or electrical, cannot take all the gyros, so there is always a surviving source of attitude or heading information to fly on.

q: What kind of vacuum pump is it, and what protects it?
a: POH 7.17: the vacuum pump is a dry-type pump, and a shear drive protects the pump from damage, so if the drive shears the gyros become inoperative. It is engine driven, which is the point for the oral: the gyros keep turning through an alternator failure or a master-off electrical fire, because the engine, not the battery, is driving them.

q: What should the suction gauge read, and when?
a: POH 7.17: the regulator is set so the normal vacuum reads 4.8 to 5.1 inches of mercury, which provides sufficient vacuum to operate all the gyros at their rated RPM. The ground check reads it at 2000 RPM and gives the same range. Note it is 5.1, not 5.2; three places in the handbook agree on 5.1, and the regulator that sets it is behind the instrument panel.

q: What does a gradual fall in vacuum mean, and what does zero mean?
a: POH 7.17 gives the complete diagnosis. A decrease in pressure in a system that has been constant may indicate a dirty filter, dirty screens, possibly a sticky vacuum regulator or a leak in the system; zero pressure would indicate a sheared pump drive, a defective pump, possibly a defective gauge or a collapsed line. In either case the handbook wants a mechanic to check the system before further damage or failure.

q: Your suction is low in slow flight on the checkride. Is that a failure?
a: Probably not. POH 7.17 says it outright: vacuum pressure, even though set correctly, can read lower at very high altitude above 12,000 feet and at low engine RPM, usually on approach or during training maneuvers, and this is normal and should not be considered a malfunction. So a low reading during slow flight or an approach is expected, and I would reassess it at cruise RPM before calling it a failure.

q: Where does cabin heat come from?
a: POH 7.23: heat for the cabin interior and the defroster system is provided by a shroud attached to the muffler, and 7.5 adds that the dual mufflers with heater shrouds supply heated air for the cabin, the defroster and the carburetor deicing system. So all the warm air on this airplane is air that has been passed over the exhaust, which is exactly why a cracked muffler is a carbon monoxide problem.

q: Why is a cracked exhaust muffler dangerous in this airplane?
a: Because cabin heat, defrost and carburetor heat all come off shrouds on the muffler, so a crack in the exhaust lets carbon monoxide into the air that is blown at the pilot. Carbon monoxide is colorless and odorless and shows as headache, drowsiness and poor judgment. The handbook's response to smoke or fumes in the cabin is in the Section 3 fire procedures: vents open, cabin heat off, and land.

q: Tell me about the seats and the restraints.
a: POH 7.25: the front seats are adjustable fore and aft and the right front seat tilts forward for access to the rear, with optional headrests and vertical adjustment. Shoulder harnesses with inertia reels are provided for each front seat occupant, and for the rear seats as standard or optional depending on the model year, which is a live question for a 1981 airplane. The Day VFR equipment list requires a safety restraint for each occupant.

q: How many cabin doors does this airplane have, and where?
a: One, on the right side. POH 7.3: on the right side of the airplane is a cabin door for entrance and exit, plus a baggage door aft of the rear seat. That single door is worth thinking about for emergency egress and briefing passengers, and it is why the open door procedure in Section 3 matters more here than on an airplane with a door each side.

q: A door pops open after takeoff. What do you do?
a: Treat it as a nuisance, not an emergency. POH 3.27: the cabin door is double latched, a partially open door will not affect normal flight characteristics, and a normal landing can be made with the door open. To close it in flight, slow to 89 KIAS, close the cabin vents and open the storm window; if the top latch is open, latch it; if the side latch is open, pull on the arm rest while moving the latch handle. If both are open, side latch first, then top.

q: Tell me about the baggage compartment.
a: POH 7.27: a 24 cubic foot baggage area behind the rear seat, with a maximum capacity of 200 pounds and an arm of 142.8 inches aft of datum, accessible from the cabin or through a large 20 by 22 inch outside baggage door. Tie-down straps are available and the handbook says they should be used at all times, with the NOTE that it is the pilot's responsibility to be sure the center of gravity falls within the allowable range.

q: There is a known typographical error in this handbook. Can you find it?
a: Yes. Section 1.15 BAGGAGE SPACE prints Maximum Ramp Weight (lbs) 22 and Maximum Landing Weight (lbs) 20, which are plainly wrong. Those two labels have been copied from 1.11 by mistake; 22 and 20 are the baggage door dimensions, as 7.27 confirms with a large 20 by 22 inch outside baggage door. Knowing that the handbook has an error in it is better evidence of reading it than reciting ten correct numbers.

q: What instruments are listed as options on this panel?
a: POH 7.19: a suction gauge, vertical speed indicator, attitude gyro, directional gyro, clock, tru-speed indicator and a turn and slip indicator or turn coordinator. Which of those are actually in this airplane has to come from the airplane and its equipment list, and it matters for a kinds-of-operation question, because the vacuum pump and gyro suction indicator are required for day IFR.

q: Does this airplane have an emergency locator transmitter?
a: POH 7.35 lists it as optional, in the aft portion of the fuselage just below the stabilator leading edge, reached through a plate on the right side held by slotted-head nylon screws. There is a three-position ON, OFF and ARM switch on the unit, normally at ARM, and a pilot remote switch on the left side panel. The handbook documents two different NARCO units, so which one is fitted here is something to confirm.

q: Is there a carburetor ice detection system on this airplane?
a: POH 7.39 describes one as optional: a control box on the instrument panel, a probe sensor mounted in the carburetor, and a red warning light to indicate the presence of ice. Its own WARNING is the part to quote: this instrument is approved as optional equipment only and flight operations should not be predicated on its use. If ice is present, the instruction is still to apply full carburetor heat.

q: Is there a gear-up landing procedure in this handbook?
a: No, and there cannot be one, because the gear is fixed: POH 7.1 calls it a single-engine, fixed gear monoplane and 7.7 refers to the fixed-gear PA-28-161. Section 3 contains no landing gear emergency of any kind. The forced landing procedure is POWER OFF LANDING, and I would say that confidently rather than improvising a gear emergency for an airplane that cannot have one.

q: Is there a ditching procedure?
a: No. Section 3 of this handbook contains engine fire during start, engine power loss during takeoff, engine power loss in flight, power off landing, fire in flight, loss of oil pressure, loss of fuel pressure, high oil temperature, electrical failures, electrical overload, spin recovery, open door, engine roughness and carburetor icing. There is no ditching procedure, so a water landing would be flown as a power off landing with the belts tight.

q: Which handbook actually applies to this airplane?
a: Piper Report VB-880. This airplane is serial 28-8116257, which falls in TCDS 2A13 item XVI-A, serials 28-7716001 through 28-8216300, and that block is covered by VB-880. The handbook circulating online for the Warrior II is VB-1180, which covers serials 28-8316001 and up. It is the right model but the wrong revision, so the systems carry across and the weights and the speeds that depend on weight do not.

q: What is the maximum takeoff weight of this airplane?
a: 2325 pounds in the normal category and 2020 pounds in utility, from FAA TCDS 2A13 item XVI-A, the item whose serial range contains 28-8116257. The widely circulated Warrior II handbook prints 2440 pounds, but that is the later serial block from 28-8316001 up and it is not this airplane. I would confirm it against Section 2 of the book actually in the airplane.

q: Someone hands you a Warrior II POH that says 2440 pounds. What do you say?
a: That it is the right model and the wrong serial block. 2440 pounds belongs to serials 28-8316001 and up, covered by report VB-1180; this airplane is 28-8116257 and TCDS 2A13 item XVI-A gives 2325 pounds normal. Everything that scales with weight goes with it: maneuvering speed, the stall speeds behind the airspeed indicator arcs, the climb and approach speeds, and all of Section 5.

q: What is the maximum ramp weight of this airplane?
a: I would take that from Section 2 of the airplane's own handbook, because it is not published anywhere I can verify. The TCDS gives no ramp weight, and the 2447 pounds in the later handbook is simply that book's 2440 pound gross plus the 7 pound start, taxi and run-up fuel allowance. I could do the same arithmetic on 2325 pounds, but the answer would be my arithmetic rather than a published limit.

q: Is the maximum landing weight the same as the takeoff weight?
a: On the later serials it is: that handbook prints the same figure for both, so there is no reduced landing weight on this type. For this airplane the likely answer is that takeoff and landing weight are both 2325 pounds, but applying that convention to a different serial block is an assumption, so I would confirm it in Section 2 of this airplane's own handbook rather than state it flatly.

q: What is maneuvering speed on this airplane?
a: It has to come from this airplane's own handbook, because maneuvering speed is quoted at a gross weight and this airplane's gross weight is not the one in the circulating book. That book gives 111 KIAS at 2440 pounds and 88 KIAS at 1531 pounds, with linear interpolation permitted; interpolating to 2325 pounds gives about 108 knots, which the square root of weight rule agrees with, but that is derived, not published.

q: Why does maneuvering speed change with weight?
a: Because a lighter airplane accelerates to the limit load factor at a lower speed. The handbook puts it in one line: maneuvering speed decreases at lighter weight as the effects of aerodynamic forces become more pronounced, linear interpolation may be used for intermediate gross weights, and maneuvering speed should not be exceeded while operating in rough air. The same relationship is why this airplane's number is lower than the 2440 pound figure.
dup: Why does Va increase with weight?

q: What does the maneuvering speed placard in the cockpit say?
a: On the later serials it reads Va equals 111 KIAS at 2440 pounds, see POH. The placard physically in this airplane will name a different weight and a different speed, because its gross weight is 2325 pounds, so I would read my own placard and quote that. Pointing out that the printed placard in the common handbook belongs to a different serial block is a good way to show I understand applicability.

q: What is turbulent air operating speed, and how does it relate to Va?
a: They are the same speed under two names. The handbook lists turbulent air operating speed in Section 4 and refers you straight back to the design maneuvering speed paragraph in Section 2. So it carries exactly the same weight dependence, and the figure for this airplane has to come from its own book rather than from the 2440 pound number printed in the later handbook.

q: What is Vne on this airplane, and how is it marked?
a: 160 KIAS, 153 KCAS, marked by the red radial line at the top of the airspeed indicator. The handbook's wording is do not exceed this speed in any operation. It is a structural and flutter speed rather than a load-factor speed, so it does not vary with weight, which makes it one of the figures that carries across to this airplane unchanged.
dup: What is Vne and how is it marked?

q: What is Vno, and what does the yellow arc mean?
a: Maximum structural cruising speed, 126 KIAS, with the yellow caution arc running from 126 to 160 KIAS. The handbook's wording is do not exceed this speed except in smooth air and then only with caution. The yellow arc is the band where the airplane can be damaged by a gust or an abrupt input, so it is for smooth air only. Vno is defined at design gross weight, so I would confirm the arc against this airplane's own book.
dup: What is Vno and what does the yellow arc mean?

q: What is Vfe on this airplane?
a: 103 KIAS, 100 KCAS, the top of the white arc, with the handbook's wording being do not exceed this speed with the flaps extended. Operating Tip 10.3(c) adds the airmanship: flaps may be lowered at airspeeds up to 103 KIAS, but to reduce flap operating loads it is desirable to have the airplane at a slower speed before extending them. The placarded landing checklist says flaps set, white arc.
dup: What is Vfe and what marks it on the airspeed indicator?

q: What does the white arc on your airspeed indicator represent?
a: The flap operating range: 44 to 103 KIAS in the circulating handbook, bottom end being the stall speed in the landing configuration and top end Vfe. The caution for this airplane is that the bottom end is a stall speed at 2440 pounds, and this airplane is lighter, so the arc its own book specifies may start lower. I would read the arcs off the actual instrument and compare them with this airplane's handbook.

q: What does the green arc represent?
a: The normal operating range, 50 to 126 KIAS in the circulating handbook, from the clean stall speed up to maximum structural cruising speed. The bottom of the green arc is a stall speed defined at 2440 pounds, which is not this airplane's gross weight, so the arc start is one of the markings to check against the instrument and against this airplane's own book.

q: How many markings are on this airspeed indicator, and is one of them blue?
a: Four markings and no blue line: one red radial at 160 KIAS, a yellow arc 126 to 160, a green arc 50 to 126 and a white arc 44 to 103. A blue radial is single-engine best rate of climb on a twin, so it does not belong on a Warrior. The caution is that three of those four endpoints are weight dependent and were set at a heavier gross weight than this airplane's.

q: Where does the handbook print Vso and Vs1?
a: It does not print them as named speeds at all. The stall speeds come out of the arcs and out of one sentence in Section 4: the gross weight stalling speed with power off and full flaps is 44 KIAS, which is also the bottom of the white arc, and 50 KIAS at the bottom of the green arc is Vs1 by convention. Both are gross weight figures at 2440 pounds, so this airplane stalls slower and its own book gives the numbers.

q: What are Vx and Vy on this airplane?
a: The circulating handbook gives best rate of climb at 79 KIAS and best angle at 63 KIAS, both explicitly at gross weight, and adds that at lighter than gross weight these speeds are reduced somewhat. Gross weight in that book means 2440 pounds, which is not this airplane's, so I would fly the speeds from this airplane's own handbook and expect them to be a little lower.

q: What approach speeds does the handbook give?
a: An initial approach speed of about 70 KIAS and a final approach speed of 63 KIAS with flaps extended to 40 degrees, with flaps able to be lowered at speeds up to 103 KIAS. Section 4.5 says plainly that the Section 4 speeds are for standard airplanes flown at gross weight under standard conditions at sea level, and that gross weight is 2440 pounds, so this airplane's own figures will be a little lower.

q: What is the best glide speed in this airplane?
a: The circulating handbook gives 73 KIAS, prop windmilling, flaps up, no wind, and the glide chart states its weight as 2440 pounds. Since this airplane is lighter, its best glide speed is lower, and the correct number comes from its own handbook. The technique does not change: trim for the published best gliding angle, pick the field, and only slow further once the field is made.
