q: What glide ratio does this airplane have?
a: No glide ratio is published anywhere in the handbook. What is published is a glide performance chart at 73 KIAS with the propeller windmilling, flaps up and no wind, and the chart's own worked example loses 3000 feet of altitude over 5.6 nautical miles. I would present that as reading the chart rather than as a published ratio, and I would say that the chart itself is drawn at a weight this airplane does not operate at.

q: What is the maximum demonstrated crosswind component?
a: 17 knots, printed in Section 4.5 and on the cockpit placard as DEMO. X-WIND 17 KTS. It is a demonstrated value rather than a limitation, so it is what a test pilot showed on a particular day, not a line the airplane cannot cross. Whether I would accept 17 knots depends on my currency and the runway, and the handbook's crosswind technique is a faster approach with partial or no flaps.

q: What are the baggage limits?
a: 200 pounds in the normal category and zero in utility. The baggage door placard says BAGGAGE MAXIMUM 200 LBS and then UTILITY CATEGORY OPERATION, NO BAGGAGE OR AFT PASSENGERS ALLOWED. The 200 pounds is a structural limit, so it is the same across the Warrior II serial range, but on a 2325 pound airplane you run out of gross weight long before you run out of baggage allowance.

q: Where is the datum on this airplane?
a: 78.4 inches ahead of the wing leading edge at the inboard intersection of the straight and tapered section, which is a geometric definition and so is the same whatever the gross weight. The loading arms are geometry too and carry across: pilot and front passenger 80.5 inches, rear seats 118.1, fuel 95.0 and baggage 142.8, all aft of datum.

q: What are the center of gravity limits?
a: The rearward limit is 93.0 inches aft of datum throughout, and the forward limit varies with weight: 83.0 inches at 1950 pounds and less, with straight line variation above that. The upper anchor printed in the circulating handbook is 88.3 inches at 2440 pounds, which is not this airplane's gross weight, so the whole upper part of its envelope comes from its own book. The utility rows are 83.8 at 2020 pounds and 83.0 at 1950 and below.

q: Does the handbook publish a moment limit table?
a: No. Section 2 gives the CG limits in inches only, and Section 6 works in weight and arm with a loading graph and a graphical center of gravity envelope. There is no moment envelope with inch-pound limits anywhere in the handbook, so any table in that form has come from another source and I would check it against the airplane's own weight and balance data before trusting it.

q: What maneuvers are prohibited in the normal category?
a: Section 2.15: all acrobatic maneuvers including spins are prohibited in the normal category. The in-full-view-of-pilot placard says the same thing twice over, that no acrobatic maneuvers are approved for normal category operations and that spins are prohibited for normal and utility category. So the commercial maneuvers that need more than 60 degrees of bank have to be flown in the utility category.

q: What maneuvers are approved in the utility category?
a: Three, for bank angles exceeding 60 degrees: steep turns, lazy eights and chandelles. Those three carry across to this airplane. What does not carry is the entry speed, because the 111 KIAS printed beside them in the circulating handbook is maneuvering speed at 2440 pounds; this airplane's entry speed is lower and comes from its own book and its own placard.

q: What else does utility category operation require?
a: No aft passengers and no baggage, per the baggage door placard and the utility category placard, which also raises the positive limit load factor from 3.8 G to 4.4 G. Spins stay prohibited in both categories. In practice that means the commercial maneuvers are flown with two people in the front, nothing in the back, and a center of gravity inside the utility envelope.

q: What are the flight load factors?
a: Section 2.17: positive 3.8 G in the normal category and 4.4 G in utility. For negative G the handbook does not print a number at all; it writes no inverted maneuvers approved across both columns. It also publishes no separate flaps-up and flaps-down load factors, so the commonly taught 2.0 G flaps-down figure is from the certification rule and not from this handbook.

q: What kinds of operation is this airplane approved for?
a: Section 2.19: day or night VFR and day or night IFR, when the appropriate equipment is installed and operable. There is no icing approval stated anywhere in Section 2, so flight into known icing is not approved. The handbook also carries an MEL statement, that certain operations may be authorized with listed equipment inoperative under a current FAA-approved Minimum Equipment List dated concurrently with or after the handbook.

q: What equipment does the handbook require for day VFR in this airplane?
a: Twelve items in Section 2.19: airspeed indicator, altimeter, magnetic compass, tachometer, oil pressure indicator, oil temperature indicator, fuel pressure indicator, fuel quantity indicator for each tank, volt-ammeter, elevator and rudder trim indicator, alternator, and a safety restraint for each occupant. The two people forget are the fuel pressure indicator and the volt-ammeter, and that list is a better answer for this airplane than reciting the regulation.

q: What is added for night VFR, and for IFR?
a: Section 2.19: night VFR adds position lights, instrument lights and anti-collision strobe lights to the day VFR list. Day IFR adds a vacuum pump and a gyro suction indicator, which is why the vacuum system being optional on this type matters. Night IFR is simply everything required for day and night VFR plus everything required for day IFR.

q: If the handbook lists required equipment, why does 91.205 still matter?
a: Because the handbook says so. The NOTE at the end of Section 2.19 reads that the above system and equipment list does not include specific flight instruments and communication and navigation equipment required by the FAR Part 91 and 135 operating requirements. So the POH list is the type certification basis and the operating rule sits on top of it; I need both to be satisfied before the airplane is legal.

q: Can you use the Section 5 performance charts out of the common handbook?
a: No. Every chart in that section is computed for a 2440 pound airplane, including takeoff ground roll and distance, climb, cruise, landing distance, glide and the stall speed chart, whose weight axis is drawn to maximum weight 2440 pounds. This airplane plans from its own book. Some of those charts do read down to lighter weights, so entering them at 2325 pounds is not nonsense, but they are not approved data for this airplane.

q: What is the wing loading and power loading of this airplane?
a: The handbook prints 14.4 pounds per square foot and 15.3 pounds per horsepower, but both are computed at 2440 pounds and are therefore not this airplane's. At 2325 pounds they work out around 13.7 and 14.5, but those are derived figures and are not published anywhere, so I would offer them as arithmetic rather than quote them as handbook values.

q: How do you do a short field takeoff in this airplane?
a: Here is the trap: the handbook's plain short field takeoff is accomplished without flaps, by applying full power before brake release, lifting off at 40 to 52 KIAS depending on weight and climbing out at 79 KIAS. It is the short field with an obstacle that uses 25 degrees, the second notch. Those speed bands are quoted at a heavier gross weight, so I would take the numbers from this airplane's own book.

q: How do you do a soft field takeoff?
a: Both soft field cases use 25 degrees of flap, the second notch. The technique is to accelerate and lift the nose gear off as soon as possible, lift off at the lowest possible airspeed, and then with an obstacle accelerate just above the ground to 52 KIAS to climb past it, or without an obstacle accelerate just above the ground to the best rate of climb speed, retracting the flaps slowly while climbing out.

q: What is the handbook's technique for a short field landing?
a: Section 4.31: the best technique for short and slow landings is to use full flap and enough power to maintain the desired airspeed and approach flight path, with mixture full rich, fuel on the fullest tank and the electric fuel pump on. Reduce speed during the flare and contact the ground close to the stalling speed, hold the nose wheel off as long as possible, then lower it gently and brake.

q: How does the handbook want a crosswind landing flown?
a: Section 4.31: in high wind conditions, particularly in strong crosswinds, it may be desirable to approach the ground at higher than normal speeds with partial or no flaps. That trades the lower touchdown speed for better control authority and less weathercocking, and it sits alongside the handbook's general guidance to vary the flap setting and touchdown speed with the surface, the wind and the loading.

q: Give me the power off landing procedure.
a: Section 3.3: locate a suitable field, establish a spiral pattern, be 1000 feet above the field at the downwind position for a normal landing approach, and when the field can easily be reached slow to the shortest-landing speed. Touch down at the lowest possible airspeed with full flaps. When committed, ignition off, master off, fuel selector off, mixture to idle cut-off and belts and harnesses tight.

q: How do you lose extra height on a forced landing in this airplane?
a: Section 3.13: excess altitude may be lost by widening your pattern, using flaps or slipping, or a combination of these. The caution that goes with slipping is Operating Tip 10.3(i): prolonged slips or skids resulting in more than 2000 feet of altitude loss can uncover the fuel outlet and interrupt the fuel flow when the tank in use is not full, which matters if the engine is still running.

q: The engine fails just after takeoff. What does the handbook actually say?
a: Section 3.3: if sufficient runway remains for a normal landing, land straight ahead; if not, maintain a safe airspeed, make only a shallow turn to avoid obstructions and use flaps as the situation requires. If enough altitude has been gained to attempt a restart: fuel selector to a tank containing fuel, electric fuel pump check on, mixture check rich, carburetor heat on, primer locked. There is no turn-back option in the book.

q: The engine fails in cruise. Walk me through it.
a: Section 3.3: fuel selector to a tank containing fuel, electric fuel pump on, mixture rich, carburetor heat on, engine gauges checked for the cause, primer checked locked, and if no fuel pressure is indicated check the selector is on a tank with fuel in it. If power returns, carb heat and pump off. If not, prepare for a power off landing and trim for best gliding angle, taking the speed from this airplane's own handbook.

q: Is there a spin recovery procedure, and what is the order?
a: Intentional spins are prohibited in this airplane, but there is a recovery: throttle idle, ailerons neutral, rudder full opposite to the direction of rotation, control wheel full forward, then rudder neutral when rotation stops and control wheel as required to smoothly regain level flight. Note Piper's order, with throttle and ailerons first, and note the word smoothly, which is there to avoid a secondary stall or an overspeed.

q: What does the category placard in full view of the pilot say?
a: THIS AIRPLANE MUST BE OPERATED AS A NORMAL OR UTILITY CATEGORY AIRPLANE IN COMPLIANCE WITH THE OPERATING LIMITATIONS STATED IN THE FORM OF PLACARDS, MARKINGS AND MANUALS. ALL MARKINGS AND PLACARDS ON THIS AIRPLANE APPLY TO ITS OPERATION AS A UTILITY CATEGORY AIRPLANE. FOR NORMAL AND UTILITY CATEGORY OPERATION, REFER TO THE PILOT'S OPERATING HANDBOOK. NO ACROBATIC MANEUVERS ARE APPROVED FOR NORMAL CATEGORY OPERATIONS. SPINS ARE PROHIBITED FOR NORMAL AND UTILITY CATEGORY.

q: What does the placarded takeoff checklist say, word for word?
a: TAKEOFF CHECKLIST: Fuel on proper tank; Seat backs erect; Electric fuel pump on; Fasten belts/harness; Engine gauges checked; Trim tab set; Flaps set; Controls free; Carb. heat off; Door latched; Mixture set; Air conditioner off; Primer locked. It is a two-column placard in full view of the pilot, and note that electric fuel pump on appears there, which makes the pump rule a placarded item rather than advice.

q: What does the placarded landing checklist say, word for word?
a: LANDING CHECKLIST: Fuel on proper tank; Flaps set (White Arc); Mixture rich; Fasten belts/harness; Electric fuel pump on; Air conditioner off; Seat backs erect. Flaps set, white arc, is the placarded way of saying do not exceed the flap limiting speed of 103 KIAS. A footnote under both placards says the air conditioner off item is mandatory for air conditioned aircraft only.

q: What does the baggage compartment placard say?
a: BAGGAGE MAXIMUM 200 LBS. UTILITY CATEGORY OPERATION - NO BAGGAGE OR AFT PASSENGERS ALLOWED. NORMAL CATEGORY OPERATION - SEE PILOT'S OPERATING HANDBOOK WEIGHT AND BALANCE SECTION FOR BAGGAGE AND AFT PASSENGER LIMITATIONS. It is on the inside of the baggage compartment door, and the 200 pound limit is structural, so it is the same for this serial as for any other Warrior II.

q: What does the utility category placard say?
a: UTILITY CATEGORY OPERATION ONLY. (1) NO AFT PASSENGERS ALLOWED. (2) ACROBATIC MANEUVERS ARE LIMITED TO THE FOLLOWING: SPINS PROHIBITED; STEEP TURNS; LAZY EIGHTS; CHANDELLES, each with an entry speed printed beside it. The three maneuvers carry across to this airplane; the entry speeds printed in the common handbook are maneuvering speed at 2440 pounds, so this airplane's placard will show its own, lower figure.

q: What does the oil cooler winterization placard say?
a: OIL COOLER WINTERIZATION PLATE TO BE REMOVED WHEN AMBIENT TEMPERATURE EXCEEDS 50 DEGREES F. It is in full view of the pilot when the winterization kit is installed, and Section 7.5 describes the plate as provided to restrict air during winter operation. For a late November checkride I would look for the plate on the preflight and know the removal rule.

q: What does the air conditioner placard say, and when does it apply?
a: WARNING - AIR CONDITIONER MUST BE OFF TO INSURE NORMAL TAKEOFF CLIMB PERFORMANCE. It is in full view of the pilot near the air conditioner control panel, and only applies when air conditioning is installed. The matching footnote under the takeoff and landing checklist placards says the air conditioner off item in those checklists is mandatory for air conditioned aircraft only.

q: What does the fuel filler placard on this airplane say?
a: FUEL - 100 OR 100LL AVIATION GRADE, adjacent to the fuel filler caps. The handbook prints a second, graphic AVGAS ONLY placard with GRADE 100LL and GRADE 100 lines, but restricts it to serial numbers 28-8316037 and up, and this airplane is 28-8116257, so it gets the first version. That is a case where the handbook does the serial-block reasoning for you.

q: Summarize the general limitations statement in Section 2.
a: Section 2.1: this airplane must be operated as a normal or utility category airplane in compliance with the operating limitations stated in the form of placards and markings and those given in this section and handbook. The point for the oral is where limitations live: not only in Section 2 but in the placards and the instrument markings as well, and all three have to agree with the airplane in front of you.

q: What are the power plant instrument markings, all of them?
a: Tachometer, green arc 500 to 2700 RPM with the red line at 2700. Oil temperature, green 75 to 245 degrees F, red line 245. Oil pressure, green 60 to 90 PSI, yellow 25 to 60 at idle, a second yellow 90 to 100 for ground warm-up, red lines at 25 and 100. Fuel pressure, green .5 to 8 PSI with red lines at .5 and 8. Those are the figures an examiner can ask for one at a time.

q: With a checkride in late November, which limitations would you check first?
a: The ones the season touches. Whether the oil cooler winterization plate is fitted, and its 50 degrees F removal rule; the oil grade for the temperature, which in the 0 to 70 degrees F row is SAE 30 straight or 30, 40 or 20W-40 ashless dispersant; carburetor ice, since the handbook's band of minus 5 to 20 degrees C covers a November morning exactly; and the weight the airplane plans to, which is 2325 pounds and not 2440.
